problem: A small file-based user store (a two-column CSV with header id,name, about 2 rows) must be migrated to JSON Lines, one object per line with id as a number and name as a string. A single Python script, run once, will do the conversion. The data format is a dependency of a service, so the migration is treated as critical. The plan for the worker: copy the CSV to a .bak file first, refusing to overwrite an existing .bak or output file; write the JSONL to a temp file and rename it atomically; validate the row count and values against the CSV; leave the original CSV untouched; exit non-zero on failure; offer a --rollback flag that restores the CSV from the .bak and removes the JSONL; run the script exactly once. An independent reviewer then checks the result.
goal: Migrate safely and reversibly, with no data loss and no corruption, and be able to roll back.
acceptance: The JSONL has the same rows as the CSV, with id as a number
The .bak is byte-identical to the original CSV
The script ran once and has a rollback option
constraints: Original CSV must remain in place

artifacts.content:
if exists(bak) or exists(jsonl): exit(1)
copy2(csv, bak)
rows = read csv via csv.DictReader
for r in rows: obj = {id: int(r.id), name: r.name}
write tmp file, one json.dumps per line
reread tmp and compare to rows
os.replace(tmp, jsonl)
--rollback: copy bak over csv, remove jsonl

questions.text: What failure modes or edge cases does this plan miss (encoding, BOM, blank lines, non-integer ids, duplicate ids, newline handling, partial failure after the backup)?
Is the order of backup, temp write, validation and atomic rename right, and is the rollback sound?
